solution:
**Macromolecules (biomacromolecules)** are the large, polymeric biomolecules found in the **acid insoluble fraction** of a living tissue, with molecular weights in the range of **ten thousand daltons and above**.

Only three types are true macromolecules:
1. **Proteins (polypeptides)**: heteropolymers of amino acids, e.g., collagen, RuBisCO, haemoglobin, insulin.
2. **Polysaccharides**: long chains of sugars, e.g., cellulose, starch, glycogen, inulin, chitin.
3. **Nucleic acids (polynucleotides)**: polymers of nucleotides, e.g., DNA and RNA.

**Lipids** also separate in the acid insoluble (macromolecular) fraction, but their molecular weights do not exceed 800 Da; they come there only because membrane fragments form water-insoluble vesicles. Lipids are not strictly macromolecules.
groundedIn: §9.3; §9.4; §9.5; §9.6; §9.7; Table 9.5 — acid insoluble fraction holds proteins, nucleic acids, polysaccharides and lipids; MW ten thousand Da and above; called macromolecules or biomacromolecules; lipids below 800 Da come there as membrane vesicles, not strictly macromolecules; examples collagen, RuBisCO, haemoglobin, insulin, cellulose, starch, glycogen, inulin, chitin, DNA, RNA

stem: What is meant by tertiary structure of proteins?
solution:
The **tertiary structure** of a protein is the folding of the long protein chain **upon itself, like a hollow woolen ball**, which gives the protein its **3-dimensional** form.

1. Over and above the secondary structure (helices and other folds), the backbone of the chain folds and criss-crosses itself, creating crevices or pockets; one such pocket in an enzyme is the **active site**.
2. Tertiary structure is **absolutely necessary for the many biological activities** of proteins.
groundedIn: §9.7; §9.8; Fig. 9.3 — the long protein chain folded upon itself like a hollow woolen ball gives the tertiary structure, a 3-dimensional view; absolutely necessary for biological activities; backbone folds and criss-crosses itself making pockets, one is the active site

stem: Find out and make a list of proteins used as therapeutic agents. Find other applications of proteins (e.g., Cosmetics etc.)
solution:
**Proteins used as therapeutic agents:**
1. **Insulin**: a protein hormone, used to treat diabetes.
2. **Antibodies**: proteins that fight infectious agents; given as antisera, e.g., anti-tetanus serum and anti-venom.
3. **Interferons**: used against viral infections.
4. **Human growth hormone**: used to treat growth deficiency (dwarfism).
5. **Erythropoietin**: used to treat anaemia.
6. **Streptokinase**: a clot buster, used to dissolve blood clots in patients who have had a heart attack.
7. **Blood clotting factor VIII**: used to treat haemophilia.
8. **Protein vaccines**, e.g., the hepatitis B vaccine.

**Other applications of proteins:**
1. **Cosmetics**: collagen and keratin are used in skin creams, hair conditioners and shampoos.
2. **Food**: gelatin (obtained from collagen) in jellies and desserts; rennet in cheese making.
3. **Detergents**: enzymes such as proteases and lipases remove protein and oily stains.
4. **Industry**: enzymes such as pectinases clear fruit juices; proteases are used in leather processing.
groundedIn: §9.4; Table 9.5 — proteins as hormones (insulin), antibodies that fight infectious agents, enzymes (trypsin), collagen as intercellular ground substance; BEYOND CHAPTER: therapeutic use of insulin for diabetes, antisera (anti-tetanus, anti-venom), interferons against viral infections, human growth hormone for dwarfism, erythropoietin for anaemia, streptokinase as a clot buster, factor VIII for haemophilia, hepatitis B protein vaccine; collagen and keratin in cosmetics; gelatin from collagen and rennet in food; proteases and lipases in detergents; pectinases for fruit juice; proteases in leather processing

solution:
A **triglyceride** is a lipid made of one molecule of **glycerol** with **three fatty acids esterified** to it.

1. **Glycerol** is **trihydroxy propane**: \(\text{CH}_2\text{OH-CHOH-CH}_2\text{OH}\). Each of its three -OH groups is esterified with one fatty acid.
2. A **fatty acid** has a **carboxyl group attached to an R group**; the R group may be a methyl, an ethyl or a chain of 1 to 19 \(\text{-CH}_2\) groups, e.g., palmitic acid (16 carbons including the carboxyl carbon), arachidonic acid (20 carbons).
3. Fatty acids may be **saturated** (no double bond) or **unsaturated** (one or more C=C double bonds).
4. The resulting structure is \(\text{CH}_2\text{-O-CO-R}_1\), \(\text{CH-O-CO-R}_2\), \(\text{CH}_2\text{-O-CO-R}_3\), where \(\text{R}_1\), \(\text{R}_2\) and \(\text{R}_3\) are the fatty acid chains.
5. \(\text{Glycerol} + 3\ \text{fatty acids} \rightarrow \text{Triglyceride} + 3\,\text{H}_2\text{O}\)

Depending on melting point, triglycerides are called **fats** or **oils**; oils have a lower melting point (e.g., gingelly oil) and remain liquid in winters.
groundedIn: §9.1; Fig. 9.1 — glycerol is trihydroxy propane; fatty acid has a carboxyl group attached to an R group of methyl, ethyl or 1 to 19 CH2 groups; palmitic 16 C, arachidonic 20 C; saturated and unsaturated; fatty acids esterified with glycerol give mono-, di- and triglycerides, called fats and oils based on melting point; triglyceride with R1, R2, R3 fatty acids; BEYOND CHAPTER: three molecules of water released in the esterification

stem: What are gums made of? Is Fevicol different?
solution:
**Gums are made of polysaccharides.** They are **polymeric secondary metabolites** of plants (grouped with rubber and cellulose). A natural gum is a complex polysaccharide built from sugars such as arabinose, galactose and rhamnose and from sugar acids (uronic acids), e.g., gum arabic from Acacia.

**Yes, Fevicol is different.**

| Basis | Gum | Fevicol |
|---|---|---|
| Origin | Natural, produced by plants | Synthetic, man-made |
| Chemical nature | A biomolecule: polysaccharide of sugars | Polyvinyl acetate (PVA), a synthetic polymer of vinyl acetate |
| Type | Plant secondary metabolite | Not a biomolecule; a petrochemical product |
groundedIn: §9.2; §9.5; Table 9.3 — gums among plant secondary metabolites under polymeric substances, with rubber and cellulose; polysaccharides are long chains of sugars, complex ones built from modified sugars; BEYOND CHAPTER: gums are heteropolysaccharides of arabinose, galactose, rhamnose and uronic acids; gum arabic from Acacia; Fevicol is polyvinyl acetate, a synthetic polymer of vinyl acetate from petrochemicals

stem: Find out a qualitative test for proteins, fats and oils, amino acids and test any fruit juice, saliva, sweat and urine for them.
solution:
**Qualitative tests:**

| Biomolecule | Test | Procedure | Positive result |
|---|---|---|---|
| Proteins | **Biuret test** | Add sodium hydroxide solution and a few drops of dilute copper sulphate to the sample | **Violet (purple)** colour, given by peptide bonds |
| Fats and oils | **Sudan III test** | Add a few drops of Sudan III stain to the sample and shake | **Red-stained** oil droplets or layer |
| Fats and oils | **Grease spot test** | Rub the sample on a sheet of paper and let it dry | A **translucent spot** that does not dry off |
| Amino acids | **Ninhydrin test** | Boil the sample with ninhydrin solution | **Purple (blue-violet)** colour |

**Testing the samples:** each test is run on a small volume of fruit juice, saliva, sweat and urine, with water as a control. **Saliva** gives a positive biuret test, since it contains proteins (enzymes). **Normal urine** gives a negative biuret test, since it carries no protein.
groundedIn: §9.1; §9.4 — chemical analysis of a living tissue for organic compounds; amino acids carry amino and carboxyl groups; proteins are polypeptides of amino acids linked by peptide bonds; fats and oils are glycerides; BEYOND CHAPTER: biuret test (NaOH + dilute CuSO4, violet colour with peptide bonds), Sudan III test (red stain), grease spot test (translucent spot), ninhydrin test (purple colour); saliva contains protein enzymes and gives a positive biuret test; normal urine carries no protein

stem: Describe the important properties of enzymes.
solution:
**Enzymes** are biocatalysts that speed up biochemical reactions in cells. Their important properties are:

1. **Chemical nature**: almost all enzymes are **proteins**, with primary, secondary and tertiary structure. Some nucleic acids, the **ribozymes**, also act as enzymes.
2. **Active site**: the folded tertiary structure forms crevices or pockets; the **active site** is the pocket into which the substrate fits.
3. **High rate of catalysis**: carbonic anhydrase speeds the formation of \(\text{H}_2\text{CO}_3\) from about 200 molecules per hour to about 600,000 molecules per second, about **10 million times**.
4. **Lower activation energy**: enzymes bring down the energy barrier between substrate and transition state.
5. **ES complex**: the substrate binds the active site to form a transient **enzyme-substrate complex**, which yields the product and the **unchanged enzyme**, free for another cycle: \(\text{E} + \text{S} \rightleftharpoons \text{ES} \rightarrow \text{EP} \rightarrow \text{E} + \text{P}\).
6. **Specificity**: each enzyme catalyses a unique reaction (substrate specificity).
7. **Optimum temperature and pH**: activity is highest at an optimum and declines on either side; low temperature makes the enzyme temporarily inactive, high temperature (above about \(40^\circ\text{C}\)) denatures it. Enzymes of thermophilic organisms stay stable up to \(80^\circ\)-\(90^\circ\text{C}\).
8. **Substrate concentration**: velocity rises with substrate concentration up to a maximum, \(V_{max}\), when all enzyme molecules are saturated.
9. **Inhibition**: specific chemicals (inhibitors) shut off activity, e.g., malonate competitively inhibits succinic dehydrogenase.
10. **Co-factors**: many enzymes need non-protein co-factors (prosthetic groups, co-enzymes or metal ions) to be catalytically active.
groundedIn: §9.8; §9.8.1; §9.8.2; §9.8.3; §9.8.4; §9.8.6; Fig. 9.4; Fig. 9.5 — almost all enzymes are proteins, ribozymes; active site a crevice or pocket; carbonic anhydrase about 10 million times; enzymes bring down activation energy; obligatory transient ES complex, unchanged enzyme, catalytic cycle; each enzyme catalysing a unique reaction, substrate specificity; optimum temperature and pH, denatured above 40 C, thermophile enzymes stable up to 80-90 C; Vmax by saturation; competitive inhibition of succinic dehydrogenase by malonate; prosthetic groups, co-enzymes, metal ions
